title: Python Fundamentals: Syntax, Types, and Control Flow

questions.question: What does it mean that Python is dynamically typed?
options: Types must be declared before a variable is used
Type checking happens at run time; names carry no type of their own
Python has no types at all
Variables are automatically converted to strings
questions.rationale: Dynamic typing means the type lives with the value and is checked at run time; a name can be rebound to objects of any type because the name itself has no type.

questions.question: Which of these values is truthy in Python?
questions.rationale: Empty containers, 0, and None are falsy, but a non-empty string such as "0" is truthy even though it denotes the digit zero.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a list and a tuple?
options: Tuples are unordered; lists are ordered
Lists are mutable; tuples are immutable
questions.rationale: Both are ordered and both can hold mixed types; the real difference is mutability — lists can change in place, tuples cannot.

questions.question: What does -7 // 2 evaluate to in Python?
questions.rationale: // is floor division, which rounds toward negative infinity, so -7 // 2 is -4, not -3 or the float -3.5.

questions.question: Why is `def add(item, basket=[])` considered dangerous?
options: The default list is created once at definition time and shared by all calls
Lists are not allowed as default values
It makes the function run more slowly
It silently converts items to strings
questions.rationale: Default values are evaluated once when the function is defined, so every caller who omits basket appends to the same list — the safe pattern is to default to None and create a fresh list inside.

questions.question: Which collection is the best choice for fast membership tests and removing duplicates?
questions.rationale: Sets store unique members and test membership in roughly constant time; lists require a linear scan and tuples are immutable records.

questions.question: What does [n * n for n in range(1, 5)] evaluate to?
questions.rationale: range(1, 5) yields 1, 2, 3, 4 (stop excluded), and the comprehension squares each, giving [1, 4, 9, 16].

questions.question: In Python, blocks of code are defined by:
options: A semicolon at the end of each line
questions.rationale: Indentation is syntax in Python: four spaces mark each block, which is why mixing tabs and spaces causes TabError.

questions.question: What does for i in range(1, 6, 2) print when iterated?
questions.rationale: range(start, stop, step) counts from 1 up to but excluding 6 in steps of 2, producing 1, 3, 5.

questions.question: A Python function with no return statement returns:
questions.rationale: Falling off the end of a function (or executing a bare return) returns None, which is why 'print inside the function' often hides a None result.
